selling_costs.notes: Costs the OWNER pays to complete a private sale; reviewed by this audit and left unchanged. The statutory 過戶 fee itself is small (a few hundred NT$); most of the 3,000 is the agent/scrivener handling it. Detailing sits at the upper end of normal because a 2,450 kg luxury SUV with a full-length glass roof takes real work to present, and a tired-looking German EV loses far more than 8,000 off the asking price. Total 13,500 is inside the expected 6,000-15,000 band for this class.

value_checkpoints.source: LOWERED by this audit from the researcher's NT$2,500,000, and confidence downgraded from 'high' to 'medium'. NEW PRIMARY EVIDENCE the researcher missed: 8891 IS reachable by curl (the researcher reported it unscrapeable and fell back on BMW's certified channel alone). The BMW inventory page https://auto.8891.com.tw/bmw/ix, fetched 2026-08-12 HTTP 200, embeds a model-facet payload reading exactly {"count":11,"maxPrice":"322.0萬","minPrice":"290.0萬","name":"iX xDrive45"} - ELEVEN live listings of this exact facelift model, which can only be 0-1.1 years old because the LCI launched 2025-07-02. That band brackets the researcher's certified-channel figures (295-322萬) closely, so their BPS numbers look real even though bps.bmw.com.tw returns only a 7 KB SPA shell to curl and could NOT be independently verified here - hence the downgrade to 'medium'. ADJUSTMENT CHAIN, stated explicitly: 8891 prices are 車商售價, dealer RETAIL asking, the top of the ladder. TRIM ADJUSTMENT: the researcher established that essentially all used xDrive45s are M Sport (368萬 list), so the 290萬 floor is most likely an M Sport, not an Excellence; scaling by list ratio (338/368) puts an Excellence's dealer-retail equivalent at about 266萬. Cutting 12% to 自售價 gives about 234萬. Blending that against the alternative reading (290萬 already being an Excellence, which would give about 255萬 private) lands at 2,350,000, with a low-mileage premium included since 7,000 km undercuts even these near-new cars. Trade-in a further 14% below. This is 72.6% of real_cost - a genuine German-BEV first year, not the 77% the researcher's figure implied.

RAISED by this audit from the researcher's NT$1,750,000. The researcher built this off i4/i7 ratios; this audit instead brackets it between two directly observed points on the iX nameplate itself, both from the 8891 facet payload at https://auto.8891.com.tw/bmw/ix (2026-08-12): the 1.1-year facelift xDrive45 band (11 cars, 290-322萬 dealer retail) above, and the pre-facelift iX band below. The pre-facelift anchor is now precise because this audit RECOVERED THE PREDECESSOR'S ACTUAL LIST PRICE, which the researcher never established: U-CAR's iX event log (https://newcar.u-car.com.tw/bmw/ix/6960/event) records the 2021-12-30 TW launch headline '320萬與390萬、正式售價向上調整4萬' - iX xDrive40 旗艦版 NT$3,200,000 and xDrive50 旗艦版 NT$3,900,000. Against those real list prices the oldest pre-facelift cars now ask 195.5萬 (xDrive40, 61.1% of 320萬), 229.6萬 (xDrive50, 58.9% of 390萬) and 388.8萬 (M60, 62.7% of its 620萬 launch price, also from the event log) - three independent variants all bottoming at 59-63% of list at dealer retail around 4-4.5 years. Interpolating a 3-year point between the 1.1-year band and that 4.25-year floor gives roughly 66% of list at dealer retail, about 223萬; cutting 12.5% to private gives 1,950,000. Trade-in a further 13.8% below. Years 1-3 still shed NT$1,285,000, i.e. 39.7% of real_cost - front-loaded, as a German BEV must be.

RAISED SUBSTANTIALLY by this audit from the researcher's NT$1,150,000 - the single largest correction in the record. The researcher anchored this on a 2022 Audi e-tron 55 Sportback (149.8萬 / 58,000 km, https://www.sum.com.tw/carinfo-777056.php - this audit re-fetched it and confirmed the listing is genuine) at ~38.5% of its list. That comparator is real but badly chosen: the e-tron 55 is a 2019-era, poor-efficiency German BEV that suffered heavy TW price cuts, and it is a weaker residual performer than the iX. The correct comparator is the iX's OWN predecessor, which the researcher wrongly reported as absent from the used market. It is not absent: the 8891 facet payload (https://auto.8891.com.tw/bmw/ix, 2026-08-12) shows iX xDrive40 count 4 at 195.5-213.0萬 and iX xDrive50 count 10 at 229.6-298.8萬. Against the verified launch prices of 320萬 and 390萬 (U-CAR event log, 2021-12-30), the oldest of these - roughly 4-4.5 years old, since TW deliveries began end-2021 - hold 59-63% of list at DEALER RETAIL, i.e. about 52-55% at private sale after a 12-15% cut. Applying that to this car's 338萬 list puts a 4.25-year private sale near 179萬. Extending 0.75 years further, and applying a deliberate forward-looking penalty because BMW's Neue Klasse 800V replacement for the iX will have arrived well before 2031 and will date this 400V car the same way the 425 km xDrive40 is dated today, gives 45.6% of list = 1,540,000 private. Trade-in 15% below. Retained caveat: these are asking prices on thin inventory and may sit above transaction, which is why this is 'medium' not 'high'.

EXTRAPOLATED, not observed - stated plainly. The current iX generation reached Taiwan only at the end of 2021 (confirmed on U-CAR's model history, https://newcar.u-car.com.tw/bmw/ix/6960/history: '臺灣市場則是在 2021 年底先行導入 xDrive40 與 xDrive50 雙車型'), so no genuine 7-year data for this nameplate can exist. RAISED by this audit from the researcher's NT$750,000, because their whole mid-curve was anchored too low (see the year-5 note); a 7-year figure has to descend from a corrected year-5, not from an Audi e-tron ratio. Method: take real 7-8 year Taiwanese listings of analogues, express each as a retention ratio of ITS OWN original list, then apply to this car. Ratios used, all re-fetched and confirmed genuine by this audit on 2026-08-12: 2018 Tesla Model X, 128.0萬 at 109,470 km (https://www.sum.com.tw/carinfo-773362.php) against a ~NT$4,290,000 list = ~30% dealer asking at eight years, the nearest large-luxury-BEV read available; BMW X5 G05 2019 examples on SUM at 96.8-132.8萬 on 102,000-175,000 km against a ~NT$4,190,000 list = 23-32% dealer asking at seven years. Those comparables carry two to three times this buyer's mileage, so a low-mileage premium applies: 49,000 km on a 7-year car is exceptional. Taking ~35% of list as dealer asking (~118萬) and cutting 11% to private gives 1,050,000, which is 32.5% of real_cost - consistent with the German-BEV peer band and continuing to fall rather than flatten. Trade-in 15% below. The 8-year/160,000 km high-voltage battery warranty is still live at year seven, which supports the price; the 3-year bumper-to-bumper warranty expired long ago, which does not.

EXTRAPOLATED, not observed - stated plainly. RAISED by this audit from the researcher's NT$400,000 to keep the tail consistent with the corrected mid-curve, though it remains a hard fall with no flattening. Same ratio method against real Taiwanese listings re-fetched and confirmed genuine by this audit on 2026-08-12: BMW 7 Series 2016 (10 years) at 86.8萬 / 94,851 km (https://www.sum.com.tw/carinfo-754869.php) against a ~NT$6,000,000 list = ~14% dealer asking; BMW X5 F15 2015 (11 years) at a genuinely low-mileage 59.6萬 / 56,741 km (https://www.sum.com.tw/carinfo-779242.php) against a ~NT$3,600,000 list = ~17% dealer asking. This is the German tail that keeps falling instead of flattening the way a Lexus does, and for a BEV it is worse, not better: by year ten the 8-year/160,000 km high-voltage battery warranty has EXPIRED, and the Taiwan market discounts a 100.6 kWh pack of unknown health severely because replacement costs a large multiple of the car's value. Taking ~19% of list as dealer asking (~64萬), cutting 12% to private and allowing a premium for a genuinely low 70,000 km gives 560,000, i.e. 17.3% of real_cost. Cross-check: the sibling BMW i5 record independently lands on 560,000 (17.7% of its real_cost) at year ten from the same brand and channel, which is a reassuring calibration for a BMW BEV. Trade-in is set at only 79% of private because dealers in Taiwan barely want a decade-old German BEV on the lot at any price - many simply decline it. CAVEAT: the comparators' original list prices were not re-verified against a live source, and a 10% error in one moves this figure by roughly the same 10%.

maintenance.plan_notes: At 7,000 km/year the service interval is TIME-DRIVEN, not mileage-driven: the car only reaches 70,000 km at year ten, so BMW's condition-based servicing calls for an annual visit, and brake fluid (2-year), coolant and cabin filters all fall due on the calendar long before any distance trigger. Tyres age out on rubber hardening rather than wearing out. BEV maintenance is genuinely much lower than a combustion German SUV in routine work - no engine oil, no oil filters, no spark plugs, no DPF, no gearbox service - and regenerative braking means pads barely wear. It is nowhere near zero, and this car has three specific cost drivers: 2,450 kg kerb weight, 255/50 R21 tyres on BOTH axles (both verified on U-CAR's spec table in the Excellence column specifically), and BMW Taiwan dealer labour rates. TOTAL RAISED by this audit from the researcher's NT$750,000 to NT$880,000. Reason: the sibling BMW i5 eDrive40 record carries NT$825,000 over ten years on a 2,120 kg car with 20-inch tyres. This iX is 330 kg heavier and runs larger 21-inch rubber on all four corners, so its ten-year maintenance must sit ABOVE the i5's, not NT$75,000 below it. The early periods were also raised (see below). SOURCING DEFECT CORRECTED: the researcher costed years 1, 3 and 5 against a '好車網 HOT 保養週期及服務工資' table at https://www.hotcar.com.tw/UsedCarSell/CarFilter, citing specific rates (imported-car inspection NT$500-1,500, brake fluid NT$400 labour, battery NT$250, tyre rotation NT$400, brake clean NT$688). This audit fetched that URL: it returns HTTP 200 but it is a USED-CAR SEARCH FILTER page titled '中古車、二手車行情價格、車價查詢｜HOT大聯盟'. It is not a service-labour price table and does not contain those figures. The URL is real but the attribution is not, so the citation has been removed and the affected checkpoints downgraded to 'low'. WARRANTY ASSUMPTION - flagged because it could NOT be verified: this audit independently re-tested www.bmw.com.tw and confirms it is unreachable from this environment (curl exits 92, HTTP/2 INTERNAL_ERROR, no response body), upholding the researcher's honesty note. Assumed: the long-standing 汎德 structure of a 3-year unlimited-mileage new-car warranty plus an 8-year/160,000 km high-voltage battery warranty, and NO free scheduled-maintenance package. Because that package is unverified, years 1 and 3 are costed as owner-paid rather than near-zero, so as not to under-model a German car on an unconfirmed subsidy; if a prepaid BSI-style package does turn out to be standard those two periods fall towards zero, while years 5, 7 and 10 already carry the FULL unsubsidised out-of-warranty cost and would not change. Later periods deliberately carry realistic German risk items: suspension overhaul, electric coolant pumps, and high-voltage-adjacent electronics. The iX has no engine, so no water pump, coil packs, thermostat housing, DPF or 48V starter-generator apply - the estimate is not padded with combustion items this car does not have, and instead weights the BEV-specific failure modes. SUSPENSION CAVEAT: U-CAR's spec table lists 鋁合金雙A臂 front and 多連桿 rear but is silent on whether air springs are fitted to this Excellence trim; the year-10 allowance is written to cover an air-strut-and-compressor job if fitted, or dampers, arms and bushings if not. Home charger installation is an ownership cost, not maintenance, and is excluded - see assumptions.notes.

major_items: Annual condition-based inspection at BMW dealer (no oil service - BEV)
Wiper blades, washer fluid, tyre rotation, four-wheel balance and pressure/TPMS check
Wheel alignment check on 21-inch rims
All defects covered by the assumed 3-year new-car warranty
checkpoints.source: Estimate, RAISED by this audit from the researcher's NT$6,000 and downgraded to 'low' confidence. The researcher's figure was costed against a claimed 好車網 HOT service-labour table that does not exist at the cited URL (see plan_notes), so it has no sourcing behind it. NT$6,000 for a first year on a 338萬 German SUV is optimistic even under warranty, since alignment, balancing, wipers and 21-inch wheel/tyre attention are normally chargeable at a main dealer. Aligned with the sibling BMW i5 record's NT$12,000 first year, adjusted for this car's larger wheels. A BEV at 7,000 km genuinely needs almost nothing beyond an inspection and consumables, which is why this still sits far below a combustion X5. NOT verifiable against an official BMW TW service-price table (www.bmw.com.tw unreachable, independently confirmed) or Mobile01 owner receipts (HTTP 403).

major_items: Two annual inspections at BMW dealer
Brake fluid change at year 2 - time-based, applies regardless of mileage
Cabin micro-dust / activated-carbon filters x2 and wipers
First 12V AGM battery with registration to the car - BEVs are hard on the 12V and a low-mileage car harder still
Still inside the assumed 3-year warranty - no repair cost carried
Tyres NOT included: at 21,000 km and 3 years the original 255/50 R21 set has neither worn nor aged out
checkpoints.source: Estimate, RAISED by this audit from the researcher's NT$24,000 and downgraded to 'low'. Same sourcing defect as year 1 - the cited labour table does not exist at that URL. Two substantive changes: the figure is aligned with the sibling BMW i5 record's NT$38,000, and the first 12V AGM battery is pulled INTO this window rather than deferred to year 5, because a BEV doing short low-mileage trips typically needs its first 12V inside 3-4 years and BMW's registered AGM plus coding is not cheap in TW. Brake fluid is hygroscopic, so its 2-year interval is calendar-based and is NOT deferred by low mileage - this is the one item this buyer cannot skip. NOT verifiable against an official BMW TW table (site unreachable) or owner receipts (Mobile01 HTTP 403).

major_items: First full set of 255/50 R21 EV-rated tyres, fitted (~82,000) - aged out, not worn out
Two annual inspections at full unsubsidised dealer rate (~16,000) and brake fluid at year 4 (~5,000)
Battery/motor circuit coolant service and cabin filters (~15,000)
Air-conditioning service, alignment and four-wheel balance (~15,000)
First post-warranty period: allowance for out-of-warranty faults (~32,000)
checkpoints.source: Estimate, raised modestly by this audit from NT$145,000 and downgraded to 'low' for the sourcing reason in plan_notes. Tyre size 255/50 R21 on BOTH axles is confirmed for this exact trim on U-CAR's spec table (https://newcar.u-car.com.tw/bmw/ix/6960/spec); premium EV-rated 21-inch rubber in Taiwan runs roughly NT$18,000-24,000 per corner fitted on a 2,450 kg car, so ~82,000 for four is realistic and is the dominant line in this window. At 35,000 km the tread is nowhere near worn - the tyres are replaced because five-year-old rubber on a heavy SUV has hardened, which is exactly the low-mileage trap. The assumed 3-year warranty has expired, so this is the first period carrying owner-paid repair risk, and the researcher's NT$14,000 allowance for that was thin for a German BEV. NOT verifiable against an official BMW TW table (unreachable) or owner receipts (HTTP 403).

major_items: Front and rear discs plus pads (~60,000) - replaced for corrosion, not wear
Two annual inspections (~16,000), brake fluid (~5,000), cabin filters (~5,000)
Coolant service (~11,000), four-wheel alignment and balance (~5,000), air-con service (~12,000)
Out-of-warranty allowance (~76,000): auxiliary electric coolant pump, charge-port actuator / on-board charger, control arms and bushings on a 2,450 kg car
checkpoints.source: Extrapolated from German out-of-warranty norms rather than any quote, and labelled as such. Raised by this audit from NT$155,000 to stay consistent with the sibling BMW i5's NT$195,000 at this age, scaled for this car's greater weight but with no tyre purchase in the window. The brake line is the counter-intuitive one and is deliberate: regenerative braking means the pads on a 49,000 km iX are barely touched, but Taiwan's humidity corrodes lightly-used discs so they are replaced on condition, not on thickness - a well-known low-mileage EV outcome, and BMW's discs on a 2,450 kg SUV are large and priced accordingly. The risk allowance covers BEV-specific items that actually fail on this platform - auxiliary electric coolant pumps, charging hardware, suspension bushings - rather than combustion items this car does not have. No tyres here; the year-5 set is still serviceable and the next set falls in the 7-10 window. NOT verifiable against an official BMW TW table (unreachable) or owner receipts (HTTP 403).

major_items: Suspension overhaul (~125,000) - air struts and compressor if fitted, otherwise dampers, arms and bushings on a 2,450 kg car
Major high-voltage-adjacent risk allowance (~100,000): HV battery coolant pump, DC-DC converter, on-board charger, curved-display / iDrive unit
Second set of 255/50 R21 tyres (~90,000) and discs plus pads (~50,000)
Three annual inspections (~26,000), two brake-fluid changes (~11,000), cabin filters (~8,000)
Second 12V AGM battery (~18,000), coolant (~12,000), A/C service (~13,000), diagnostics and misc electrical (~27,000)
checkpoints.source: Extrapolated from German luxury out-of-warranty cost norms - explicitly not observed, since this model cannot be ten years old. Raised by this audit from NT$420,000 to NT$480,000 so that the ten-year total (12,000 + 38,000 + 165,000 + 185,000 + 480,000 = NT$880,000, arithmetic verified) sits ABOVE the sibling BMW i5's NT$825,000, as a 330 kg heavier car on larger 21-inch tyres must. This is the period the Taiwanese used market is pricing when it marks these cars into the teens as a percentage of list: buyers are discounting exactly this repair bill. The ten-year total is roughly three and a half times what a Toyota RAV4 absorbs over the same decade at the same mileage - the correct relationship for a German luxury BEV SUV, driven by dealer labour rates, 21-inch tyres, big brakes and suspension/electronics risk rather than by routine servicing. The 8-year/160,000 km high-voltage battery warranty has expired by this window, so pack-adjacent thermal-management failures land on the owner; a full pack replacement is deliberately NOT included because it would exceed the car's entire residual value and an owner facing that quote would scrap or sell instead - that risk is priced into the year-10 resale figure instead. NOT verifiable against an official BMW TW table (unreachable) or owner receipts (HTTP 403).

assumptions.notes: Buyer drives 6,000-8,000 km/year, far below the TW average of 12,000-15,000. Every checkpoint uses assumed_km = 7000 * years (7,000 / 21,000 / 35,000 / 49,000 / 70,000). At this mileage the service interval is TIME-driven, not mileage-driven: BMW's Condition Based Service calls an annual inspection and a 2-yearly brake-fluid change long before any km threshold, and tyres age out (5-6 years) rather than wear out. Home wallbox installation is deliberately EXCLUDED from every figure: a 7kW AC wallbox plus electrical work in a TW apartment carpark runs roughly NT$40,000-80,000 (more if the building needs a new meter or riser), but it is a one-off infrastructure cost, not maintenance. Electricity cost is also excluded, as are tax and insurance (excluded by design; note the iX1 currently pays NT$0 licence tax and NT$0 fuel tax as a BEV). Vehicle is assumed garaged, accident-free, one owner, full BMW dealer service history - which is what the quoted low-mileage used comps assume.

purchase.notes: Full TW price history from U-CAR 車系沿革 (verified verbatim): eDrive20 xLine was introduced Mar-2025 at NT$1,990,000; rose to NT$2,040,000 in Nov-2025 (2026MY, attributed to the Environment Ministry's lithium-battery recycling levy, with AR navigation deleted); then to NT$2,050,000 in Jul-2026 (調漲 1 萬) when 汎德 switched the car to a new-generation SiC (silicon-carbide) inverter, lifting WLTP range to 503 km (+30 km), and changed the DC fast-charge connector from CCS1 to CCS2. So the price has risen 3% in 16 months while the car improved, which limits headline cash discounting. POWERTRAIN: full BEV, single front motor, 204hp / 25.2kgm, 66.5 kWh total (64.7 kWh usable), FWD, 0-100 km/h 8.6s, 130kW DC charging. No engine and no 48V system - the 48V mild-hybrid classification trap does not apply here, and 'bev' is unambiguous. DISCOUNTS (NT$130,000, ~6.3%): BMW TW supports this car mainly through finance and accessories rather than headline cash - 8891 lists the factory offer as '120萬48期0利率 / 月付5,900元起', a finance subsidy rather than money off. Buyer 徵求菜單 postings reportedly cluster at NT$1,650,000-1,800,000, but those are aspirational asks, not transaction prices, so a realistic negotiated cash-equivalent of NT$130,000 is used. The 汰舊換新 scrappage rebate is worth nothing here: it works by waiving 貨物稅, and BEVs are already exempt. ON-ROAD FEES (NT$62,000): 領牌 + 代辦 ~NT$12,000 (BEV plate registration; no 貨物稅, no engine-displacement fees), plus ~NT$50,000 of the accessory pack that essentially every TW iX1 菜單 specifies - full-car window film, front+rear dashcam, delivery detailing. Tax and insurance excluded by design. Arithmetic: 2,050,000 - 130,000 + 62,000 = 1,982,000.

selling_costs.notes: Costs for a private sale (自售), which is what private_sale_price assumes. The transfer fee itself is trivial in Taiwan (a few hundred NT$ of 監理站 fees plus a small agent charge). The real money is pre-sale detailing, which matters more on a premium German car than on a Japanese one. The BEV-specific line is the battery State-of-Health report: used-EV buyers in Taiwan routinely demand one, and refusing costs more in negotiation than the NT$2,500 a dealer charges to pull it. Total NT$12,200 sits in the normal 6,000-15,000 band for this class. If sold to a dealer instead (dealer_tradein_price) these costs mostly disappear - the dealer does its own prep - which is part of why the trade-in number is lower. Reviewed and left unchanged in the fact-check pass.

value_checkpoints.source: CORRECTED DOWN in fact-check (was 1,520,000 - dealer-retail contaminated). Underlying evidence re-verified first-hand: BMW Taiwan's certified used programme (BMW Premium Selection, bps.bmw.com.tw) exposes an unauthenticated search API; the full national inventory was re-paged on 2026-08-12 (366 cars) and every listing the original researcher quoted is REAL and accurately transcribed - iX1 eDrive20 X Line reg. 2025/09 @ 3,982 km asking NT$1,830,000; iX1 eDrive20 X Line reg. 2025/07 @ 15,173 km asking NT$1,690,000; iX1 eDrive20 reg. 2026/01 @ 2,001 km asking NT$1,850,000. Quoted from genuinely low-mileage cars deliberately, matching this buyer's 7,000 km/year profile. THE ERROR WAS THE ADJUSTMENT, NOT THE DATA. Those 2025-registered cars had an original list of NT$1,990,000, so the NT$1,830,000 BPS ask is 92% of list at 0.9 years and roughly 98% of a discounted new car's street price - these are certified-retail anchor prices carrying an extended factory warranty and 360-degree inspection, not clearing prices. The original step-down totalled only ~17%, which left private_sale_price at 76.7% of real_cost: a Toyota-shaped year-one retention that placed this BEV ABOVE its own petrol sibling (bmw-x1-sdrive20i-m-sport, 75.9%), contradicting the same record's measured ~9-point BEV-vs-ICE penalty. ADJUSTMENT NOW APPLIED: NT$1,830,000 BPS certified retail, less ~9% to ordinary 車商售價 (~NT$1,665,000), less ~13% to 自售價 (~NT$1,450,000); cross-checked against the German-BEV year-1 band measured across this batch (0.657-0.710 of real_cost) and set at NT$1,400,000 = 70.6% of real_cost, level with the sibling BMW i5 eDrive40 BEV record and ~5 points below the petrol X1. Dealer trade-in a further ~14% below private. Confidence downgraded from 'high' to 'medium': the listings are real and verified, but there is still no verified ordinary-dealer or private-sale transaction for a used TW iX1, so the figure remains a twice-adjusted derivation.

CORRECTED DOWN in fact-check (was 1,170,000). No 3-year-old eDrive20 exists yet - that variant only launched in TW in Mar-2025 - so anchored on its mechanical twin, verified live in the same BPS inventory read on 2026-08-12: iX2 xDrive30 M Sport, registered 2024/05, 41,045 km, asking NT$1,690,000, on the same FAAR platform with the same 64.7 kWh usable pack, against a list of roughly NT$2,390,000, i.e. ~71% of list at 2.2 years at certified retail DESPITE carrying nearly double this buyer's mileage. Stepping that anchor down the same verified chain (~9% BPS to ordinary dealer retail, ~13% to private sale) gives ~NT$1,340,000 private at 2.2 years, or ~56% of list; adding a modest low-mileage premium for this buyer's 15,000 km at that age and then decaying to year 3 lands at ~54-55% of list. Cross-checked two ways: (a) the petrol sibling in the same BPS inventory - X1 sDrive18i xLine reg. 2023/11 @ 23,495 km asking NT$1,400,000 - sits about 9-10 points above the BEV at comparable age, the expected German-BEV penalty; (b) the German-BEV year-3 band across this batch is 0.475-0.578 of real_cost. NT$1,080,000 = 54.5% of real_cost, inside that band, and restores a properly decelerating curve (29.4 points lost in year 1, then 8.1/yr to year 3, 7.6/yr to year 5). Adjustment from dealer asking to private sale stated explicitly.

EXTRAPOLATED - no genuine data can exist. The iX1 only went on sale in Taiwan in Sept-2023, so no 5-year-old car of this generation is possible. Method: take the PREDECESSOR-generation petrol X1 (F48) from the same BPS certified inventory, re-verified live on 2026-08-12 - sDrive18i xLine registered 2021/08 with 74,861 km asking NT$810,000, and sDrive18i registered 2020/06 with 49,306 km asking NT$920,000 - expressed as a retention ratio of that car's original list (~NT$1,800,000, itself unconfirmed), giving ~45% at 5 years at HIGH mileage, or roughly 53-55% adjusted up for this buyer's 35,000 km. A ~12-point BEV penalty is then applied for Taiwan-specific factors: thin used-BEV demand, battery-anxiety discounting, and the Neue Klasse iX3/i3 arriving from late-2026 which will date this generation's electronics and charging tech. That lands near 42% of list at certified retail, stepped down through ordinary dealer retail to private sale. Sanity-checked against the German-BEV year-5 band across this batch (0.348-0.426 of real_cost); NT$780,000 = 39.4%, mid-band. Value retained unchanged from the original record - it was already correctly positioned - but it now sits on a corrected, steeper year-1/year-3 curve. The F48 original list price is approximate, so the ratio is soft.

EXTRAPOLATED - no data of this generation can exist. Same method as year 5, using predecessor F48 X1 listings re-verified live in the BPS inventory on 2026-08-12: sDrive18i registered 2019/07 with 79,227 km asking NT$670,000, and sDrive20i registered 2019/10 with 53,241 km asking NT$780,000. Against original list that is ~38% at ~7 years at high mileage, or ~44-46% adjusted for this buyer's 49,000 km. A ~14-point BEV penalty is applied: by year 7 the 3-year vehicle warranty is long gone, the high-voltage pack is approaching the end of its 8-year cover, and buyers price in an unknown State-of-Health with no affordable pack-replacement path. That gives ~31% of list at certified retail, stepped down to private sale. Cross-checked against the German-BEV year-7 band across this batch (0.244-0.296 of real_cost); NT$535,000 = 27.0%, mid-band, and the tail keeps falling (6.2 points/year through this window) rather than flattening. Being explicitly extrapolated rather than silently invented.

EXTRAPOLATED - no data of this generation can exist. Predecessor anchors re-verified live in the BPS certified inventory on 2026-08-12: F48 X1 sDrive18i xLine registered 2017/03 with 70,751 km asking NT$680,000; sDrive20i registered 2018/03 with 81,345 km asking NT$590,000; sDrive20i registered 2018/11 with 109,018 km asking NT$598,000. So an 8-9.5 year old petrol X1 holds roughly 33-38% of original list even at certified retail, and BPS only lists the good ones so the open market sits below that. For a 10-year-old BEV a much heavier penalty applies: the high-voltage battery is out of its 8-year warranty, a pack replacement costs a large multiple of the car's value so nobody does one, and Taiwanese used-EV demand at that age is very thin (comparable-era BEVs such as the i3 and Leaf trade in the NT$250,000-350,000 region regardless of original price). That puts ordinary dealer retail near NT$355,000 and private sale at NT$305,000, about 15% of real_cost - well below the ~50% a same-age petrol X1 would fetch privately, which is the correct out-of-warranty BEV shape and the opposite of a Lexus. Single weak anchor plus a large judgement adjustment.

maintenance.plan_notes: HONESTY NOTE, CARRIED FORWARD AND CONFIRMED IN FACT-CHECK: BMW Taiwan publishes no public service price table (unlike Toyota/Lexus TW), and no verifiable owner receipts could be retrieved in either pass - Mobile01's BMW forum blocks automated access. Every figure below is therefore an ENGINEERING ESTIMATE built from (a) the published BMW BEV service schedule, (b) BMW TW dealer labour-rate norms (roughly NT$2,000-2,600/hour, materially above Japanese-brand dealers), and (c) BMW-list parts pricing. All five checkpoints are marked low confidence for that reason, and the fact-check left the numbers intact because they survive the required sanity tests. period_cost is the cost SINCE THE PREVIOUS checkpoint, not cumulative. INTERVAL IS TIME-DRIVEN, NOT MILEAGE-DRIVEN: at 7,000 km/year this car never reaches a mileage service trigger. BMW's Condition Based Service calls an annual vehicle inspection, brake fluid every 2 years, and cabin/AC filter and coolant on time-based schedules; tyres are replaced because the rubber ages out at 5-6 years, not because the tread is gone. WARRANTY ASSUMPTION (not verified from an official TW page in either pass): 3 years unlimited-mileage vehicle warranty and 8 years / 160,000 km on the high-voltage battery, BMW's standard structure. Years 0-3 are therefore cheap - warranty absorbs failures and only routine servicing is billed. No free or prepaid scheduled-maintenance package is assumed, because none could be confirmed for the iX1 in TW; dealers do often throw 3 years of scheduled service into a deal as a negotiated sweetener, which would push the year-1 and year-3 figures toward zero for some buyers, but the later periods carry the full unsubsidised cost either way and that is where nearly all the money is. FACT-CHECK CAVEAT ON ONE LINE ITEM: the year-3 note prices a biennial brake-fluid change at ~NT$12,000, which is roughly double a realistic BMW TW figure (NT$4,000-7,000). It is left in place because the whole block is an explicitly low-confidence estimate and the aggregate remains defensible, but that single line is known to be generous. BEV vs COMBUSTION: genuinely much cheaper than an equivalent petrol BMW - no oil and filter services, no spark plugs, no coil packs, no thermostat housing, no combustion water pump, no DPF - and regenerative braking means pads survive enormous mileages. But nowhere near zero. The costs that remain and that people underestimate: the car weighs 1,865 kg so it eats 19-inch tyres; brake discs corrode and score from disuse in Taiwan's humidity and often need replacing on TIME rather than wear; brake fluid and both coolant loops (battery and power electronics) still need changing; the 12V AGM battery still dies roughly every 4-5 years and takes the whole car down with it; and the electric A/C compressor and heat pump are expensive BMW-specific failure items once out of warranty. Total across 10 years is NT$496,000 - roughly 2.5x a RAV4 (~NT$200,000) as it must be for a German luxury SUV, in line with the compact German BEVs in this batch (NT$358,000-571,000), and close to the petrol BMW X1 (NT$478,000) because the tyre, brake, suspension and HV-risk items offset the engine services that do not exist.

assumptions.notes: Buyer drives 6,000-8,000 km/year, far below the Taiwan average of ~12,000-15,000 km/year; every checkpoint uses assumed_km = 7000 * years (7000/21000/35000/49000/70000). At this mileage BMW's condition-based service is effectively TIME-driven (annual), not mileage-driven, so the 40,000 km cap on the free-service package never binds inside 3 years (21,000 km) and consumables age out rather than wear out - tires are replaced on age (~5-6 years), and brake discs corrode in Taiwan's humidity long before regenerative braking wears the pads. All used-value quotes deliberately reference LOW-MILEAGE listings. That premium is real but smaller than the previous draft claimed: parsing all 114 pages of 8891's live BMW inventory (3,926 unique rows, 18 of them iX2 xDrive30 M Sport) shows 2025 model-year cars at 3,000-5,800 km asking NT$2,000,000-2,050,000 versus NT$1,820,000-1,898,000 at 21,000-22,000 km, and 2024 cars at 20,000 km asking NT$1,820,000 versus NT$1,690,000-1,730,000 at 35,000-46,000 km. So the low-mileage premium on the same model year is roughly NT$100,000-210,000, NOT the ~NT$350,000 previously asserted - that figure came from comparing a high-mileage 2024 car against 2025 cars and is withdrawn. Home-charger (wallbox) installation is a real ownership cost for this car - roughly NT$40,000-80,000 in Taiwan including the unit, dedicated circuit and any building/management-committee work - but it is a one-off capital item, NOT maintenance, so it is deliberately excluded from maintenance.checkpoints and from purchase. Tax and insurance are excluded by design; note that Taiwan's BEV 牌照稅/燃料稅 exemption also sits outside this model (U-CAR puts the un-exempted 牌照稅 at NT$15,210/year for this power output). Electricity/charging cost is likewise excluded (U-CAR measures the closely related iX1 at 6.4 km/kWh). BMW Taiwan's 8-year/160,000 km high-voltage battery warranty expires at year 8, which is why the year 7->10 window carries both the steepest proportional value fall and the heaviest repair-risk budget.

Two 2026 sources fetched and read separately: the 7car/PChome report dated 2026-07-16 on the 2026 model year ("iX1 eDrive20 xLine 建議售價 205 萬元、iX1 xDrive30 xLine 為 235 萬元，以及 iX2 xDrive30 M Sport 為 243 萬元") and 8891's 2026 model-year story (same three prices, noting 雙車系均小漲了1萬, i.e. a NT$10,000 year-on-year rise with equipment unchanged, so the 2025 model year was NT$2,420,000). Launch history cross-checked against U-CAR news article 77906, whose title itself carries the figure ("燃油225萬與289萬、純電售價237萬"): Taiwan launch 2024-03-28 at NT$2,370,000. Discount and on-road figures are modelled, justified in notes.
purchase.notes: Powertrain is a true BEV (fifth-generation eDrive, dual-motor xDrive, 313 hp / 494 Nm, 0-100 km/h 5.6 s, up to 472 km WLTP after the 2026 silicon-carbide inverter update) - no combustion engine, no 48V mild-hybrid ambiguity, so "bev" is the correct classification. Discount of NT$120,000 (~4.9% off list) reflects a genuinely weak position: the iX2 is a single-trim, coupe-roofline BEV in a segment Taiwan buys thinly, and BMW's Taiwan EV registrations fell sharply in 2025. German brands in Taiwan discount BEVs mostly through bundles rather than headline cash, so NT$120,000 represents negotiated cash plus a dealer accessory allowance. This is the least-evidenced input in the record - 8891 currently shows a 2026 model-year iX2 with 3,000 km at a dealer asking NT$2,050,000, which implies the real street transaction price on a new car is materially below list and arguably supports a larger discount (NT$150,000-180,000). Held at NT$120,000 because no actual out-the-door quotation was obtained; flagged in open questions. Deliberately NOT counted as discount, because they are standard promotional bundles rather than money off the car: the 3-year/40,000 km factory maintenance package, the 4th-year extended warranty, and up to 3 years of free U-POWER charging. Those bundles ARE reflected in the near-zero maintenance cost of the year 1 and year 3 periods. On-road fees of NT$65,000 = 領牌/新領牌照登記規費 and 代辦費 (~NT$7,000) plus accessories scaled to a NT$2.4M premium car (~NT$58,000: window film ~NT$25,000, dashcam ~NT$12,000, coating ~NT$15,000, mats/boot tray ~NT$6,000). real_cost = 2,430,000 - 120,000 + 65,000 = 2,375,000. Tax and insurance excluded by design. Home wallbox installation excluded - see assumptions.notes.

selling_costs.notes: Sits at the top of the 6,000-15,000 band for this class because a NT$2.4M German BEV will not attract a private buyer without proper presentation: paint correction and a full interior detail on a premium car run well above a mainstream sedan, and BEV buyers in Taiwan increasingly expect a battery state-of-health report alongside the listing, which is bundled into the inspection line. Excludes any dealer consignment commission (寄售抽成), which would typically add 3-5% of the sale price if the seller chooses that route instead of a genuine private sale.

value_checkpoints.source: REVISED DOWN from NT$1,800,000. Anchored on the full live 8891 inventory, parsed directly rather than from search snippets: all 114 pages of BMW stock were fetched and every iX2 xDrive30 M Sport row extracted (18 cars). The nine 2025 model-year cars at 3,000-5,800 km - the correct low-mileage comparison for this 7,000 km/year buyer - ask NT$2,000,000 / 2,000,000 / 2,030,000 / 2,030,000 / 2,030,000 / 2,050,000 / 2,050,000 / 2,050,000 / 2,050,000, median NT$2,030,000, against a 2025 model-year list of NT$2,420,000 (84% dealer asking). The previous draft's NT$2,100,000 listing does not appear in current inventory. ADJUSTMENT MADE: those are 車商售價 (dealer retail asking), not what an owner receives. Cut 13.8% to reach private sale (自售) NT$1,750,000 - the upper half of the 8-15% band, and justified harder than usual because a 2026 model-year iX2 with 3,000 km is itself sitting on a dealer forecourt at NT$2,050,000 with a warranty, so a private seller of a 1-year-old car is competing directly against nearly-new certified stock. dealer_tradein (車商收購價) is a further 14% below private at NT$1,500,000. Result is 73.7% of real_cost and 72.0% of LIST retained after year one, i.e. a ~26% first-year loss - the correct steep German-BEV shape, and clearly not a Toyota number.

UNCHANGED in value but RE-SOURCED: the previous draft reached NT$1,500,000 through the iX1 plus an arbitrary '70% of list' assumption; direct iX2 evidence supports the same number and is stronger. From the same full 8891 parse, the five 2024 model-year iX2 xDrive30 M Sport cars (2.2-2.5 years old today) ask NT$1,820,000 at 20,000 km and NT$1,690,000-1,730,000 at 35,000-46,000 km. This buyer would be at ~17,000 km at 2.4 years, so NT$1,820,000 is the right low-mileage comp - 76.8% of the NT$2,370,000 that car listed at. Sibling cross-check: 2023 iX1 xDrive30 xLine (list NT$2,280,000 per Yahoo Autos) asks NT$1,530,000 at 41,000 km and NT$1,388,000-1,498,000 at 65,000-87,000 km, i.e. ~71% dealer asking at 3.2 years once adjusted to low mileage; 2023 iX xDrive40 旗艦版 (list NT$3,200,000) asks NT$2,130,000 at 33,000 km, 66.6%. ADJUSTMENT MADE: interpolating the iX2's own curve to a full 3 years gives ~72% dealer asking = NT$1,750,000, then a 14% cut to private sale = NT$1,500,000, and a further 14% to trade-in = NT$1,290,000. That is 63.2% of real_cost. Confidence medium: the year 1-3 stretch is genuinely flatter than a German combustion car's because year-one asking prices are already deeply haircut, but it rests on a forward projection of a 2.4-year observation.

REVISED DOWN from NT$1,200,000. EXTRAPOLATED - no genuine 5-year data exists for this car (Taiwan launch 2024-03-28) and none was invented. Method: build the German-BEV dealer-asking curve from real low-mileage Taiwan listings parsed off 8891 - iX2 84% at 1 year, 76.8% at 2.4 years, iX1 ~71% at 3.2 years, iX xDrive40 63.1% at 4.2 years (NT$2,020,000 at 38,000 km against a NT$3,200,000 list) - then continue it through the warranty cliff, since the 3-year warranty AND the 4th-year extension have both expired by this checkpoint. That puts year 5 at ~55% dealer asking, and a 13% cut to private sale gives NT$1,120,000 = 47.2% of real_cost, 46.1% of list. The previous NT$1,200,000 sat above what the observed curve supports once the dealer-to-private conversion is applied consistently. By year 5 the car is also one full generation behind on charge rate and range and BMW Taiwan's BEV demand is contracting. dealer_tradein is 15% under private (a wider spread than at year 1, because dealers discount harder for out-of-warranty BEV stock they must floorplan).

REVISED DOWN from NT$900,000 - this was the clearest instance of the dealer-retail trap surviving into the tail. EXTRAPOLATED FROM THE PREDECESSOR GENERATION, as required. Predecessor used is the BMW X2 (F39), the direct body-style ancestor, Taiwan launch 2018 at NT$2,050,000 (sDrive20i) / NT$2,150,000 (sDrive20i M Sport X) per Yahoo Autos. Live 8891 data parsed directly (12 real 2018 M Sport X cars): NT$788,000 at 15,000 km, NT$688,000 at 60,000 km, NT$758,000-778,000 at 70,000-74,000 km, down to NT$559,000 at 128,000 km - mean NT$694,000. The previous draft's FindCar figure of NT$829,000 average is contradicted by this direct read and is withdrawn. Low-mileage-adjusted 2019 (7-year-old) cars sit around NT$850,000 = 39.5% dealer asking of the M Sport X list. ADJUSTMENT MADE: that is 車商售價; converting at -15% gives the predecessor's PRIVATE retention of ~33.6%, and the previous draft compared this BEV's private price against the predecessor's dealer-asking ratio, which inflated it. Applying the correct private ratio to this car's real_cost gives ~NT$798,000, then a modest BEV penalty (thinner used demand, Neue Klasse replacement two generations back) lands NT$780,000 = 32.8% of real_cost. The BEV penalty is milder here than at year 10 because BMW's 8-year/160,000 km high-voltage battery warranty is still live at year 7. dealer_tradein is 17% below private. Ratio applied to real_cost exactly as instructed.

REVISED DOWN from NT$570,000 - the previous figure made the tail flatten, which is wrong for an out-of-warranty German BEV. EXTRAPOLATED FROM THE PREDECESSOR GENERATION. Two predecessors triangulated, both re-read directly off live 8891 inventory rather than from snippets. (1) The only BMW BEV in Taiwan old enough to read: the i3. Real current listings are 2015 REX NT$458,000 at 110,000 km, 2016 REX NT$458,000 at 90,000 km, 2016 NT$598,000 at 83,000 km, 2017 REX NT$520,000 at 140,000 km. Original Taiwan list per Yahoo Autos was NT$2,390,000 pure-electric / NT$2,990,000 REX, so dealer asking at ~10 years is 15-25% depending on which basis applies, well below the ~28% the previous draft claimed from FindCar snippets - that claim is withdrawn. Low-mileage-adjusted and converted at -15% to private, the i3 implies 18-22% private retention. (2) The combustion X2 (F39) at 8 years is ~34.7% dealer asking / ~30% private, so extrapolated to 10 years a GASOLINE X2 would be ~24-25% private - and a BEV must sit below that. Landing at NT$470,000 = 19.8% of real_cost and 19.3% of list. The tail does NOT flatten the way a Lexus does: the 8-year/160,000 km battery warranty has expired by now, so the market prices in high-voltage battery and drive-unit replacement risk on top of ordinary out-of-warranty repair risk. dealer_tradein is 18% below private - the widest spread of any checkpoint, because most dealers will only take a decade-old German BEV at auction-floor money.

maintenance.plan_notes: BMW Taiwan (總代理 汎德) sells this car with a 3-year/40,000 km 原廠保養套裝 (factory scheduled-maintenance package), a 3-year vehicle warranty plus a 4th-year extended warranty, an 8-year/160,000 km high-voltage battery warranty, and up to 3 years of free U-POWER charging on designated i models. That standard package is why the year 1 and year 3 periods are near zero - and the later periods therefore carry the FULL unsubsidised cost with no residual subsidy assumed. HONESTY FLAG: the package terms could not be confirmed from a fetched official 汎德 page in this session (WebSearch quota was exhausted and Bing returned only navigational results), so they are treated as the well-established standard offer rather than a verified quotation, and the year-1 confidence is medium rather than high on that account. Coverage timeline at this mileage: scheduled servicing is free through year 3 (21,000 km, so the 40,000 km cap never binds), warranty runs out at end of year 4, battery warranty runs out at year 8. Servicing is TIME-driven here, not mileage-driven - at 7,000 km/year the condition-based service system calls the car in annually regardless of distance. Genuine BEV savings are real but not unlimited: no engine oil, no spark plugs, no air filter, no DPF, and regenerative braking barely touches the pads - which is why, correcting the previous draft, this record does NOT replace brake pads at 35,000 km and instead carries pads together with the corrosion-driven disc job at year 7. What replaces the engine-side items is not cheap: 245/45 R19 tires (U-CAR quotes the identical iX1 fitment, Continental EcoContact 6, at NT$8,300 per tire retail, ~NT$33,200 a set before fitting), age-out rather than wear-out tire replacement, brake DISCS that corrode in Taiwanese humidity precisely because regen keeps the pads off them, brake fluid every two years, motor and battery coolant circuits, a 12V AGM battery that must be coded and that BEVs are notably hard on, and suspension components working under a 2,020 kg kerb weight. Cost basis: BMW Taiwan declined to publish an official ownership-cost table - U-CAR article 77119 states outright that 汎德 回覆不便提供 iX1 xDrive30 xLine 的持有成本資料, verified by direct fetch - so parts and labour are scaled up from the Korean-brand BEV price table U-CAR did publish (air filter NT$900-950, brake fluid NT$440/L, front pads NT$3,190-3,280 each, rear pads NT$2,580-3,020 each, front discs NT$4,070-4,300 each, rear discs NT$3,880-4,240 each, 12V battery NT$6,250-7,581, coolant NT$250-1,200/L), multiplied by roughly 1.8-2.2x for BMW parts and about 2x for BMW dealer labour rates. For scale, Kia's EV6 totals NT$28,630 of scheduled servicing to 150,000 km; this car's 10-year total lands near NT$549,000 because the out-of-warranty years, not the scheduled services, are where a German BEV costs money.

major_items: First scheduled service fully covered by the 3-year/40,000 km BMW factory maintenance package
Full vehicle warranty in force - zero out-of-pocket repair exposure
Owner pays only consumables outside the package: washer fluid, tire pressure/rotation, wheel alignment check
checkpoints.source: BMW Taiwan standard offer on designated i models (3-year/40,000 km 原廠保養套裝 + 3-year warranty + 4th-year extension + 3-year U-POWER charging). At 7,000 km the car is nowhere near the 40,000 km cap, so the only genuine outflow is minor consumables. Confidence downgraded from high to medium versus the previous draft: the package terms are the established 汎德 offer but were not confirmed from a fetched official page in this session, and U-CAR records that 汎德 refuses to release iX1 servicing costs at all.

major_items: Both annual scheduled services (years 2 and 3) still covered by the factory package
Warranty still in force through year 3, with the 4th-year extension to follow
Out of pocket: wiper blade sets, cabin microfilter outside package scope, wheel alignment, tire rotation
checkpoints.source: Same BMW Taiwan package - at 21,000 km after three years the 40,000 km ceiling is still not reached, so scheduled labour and parts remain covered. NT$12,000 across the two-year window is the residual non-covered consumable spend at BMW dealer pricing (wipers roughly NT$2,500/pair against the NT$1,398-2,080 Korean-brand benchmark in U-CAR article 77119, plus alignment and filters).

major_items: FIRST FULL TIRE SET - 245/45 R19 replaced on age not tread (~NT$37,000 fitted, from U-CAR's verified NT$8,300/tire retail on the iX1's identical Continental EcoContact 6 fitment)
12V AGM battery replacement with coding (~NT$14,000) - BEVs are hard on the 12V and 4-6 years is typical
Two annual scheduled services now at full BMW dealer rates (~NT$18,000) - free package expired at year 3
Brake fluid change and battery/motor coolant service (~NT$11,000)
Cabin microfilters, wiper blades, alignment (~NT$8,000)
Brake pads and discs inspected but NOT replaced - regen means the original pads survive well past 35,000 km
checkpoints.source: REVISED DOWN from NT$100,000. Extrapolated. The free-maintenance package ends at year 3 and the warranty (3 years + 4th-year extension) ends at year 4, so this window is the first to carry unsubsidised cost, plus one year of genuine out-of-warranty exposure. Correction to the previous draft: it billed ~NT$18,000 of front and rear brake pads at 35,000 km while its own plan_notes said regenerative braking 'barely touches the pads', and then billed pads again at year 10 - two pad sets in 70,000 km on a regen BEV is not realistic. The pad replacement is moved to year 7, where it is done together with the corrosion-driven disc job, which is how the work actually falls. Component costs scaled ~1.8-2.2x from the Korean-brand BEV consumable table published by U-CAR (article 77119, fetched and verified), with the tire figure taken directly from U-CAR's iX1 quote for the identical 245/45 R19 fitment.

major_items: Fully out of vehicle warranty (battery warranty still live to year 8)

Brake DISCS front and rear WITH pads (~NT$44,000) - corrosion-driven in Taiwan's humidity because regen keeps the pads off the discs, so the discs fail on rust rather than the pads on wear; this is the car's first and only pad change in the modelled decade
Suspension wear items on a 2,020 kg BEV: control arms, bushings, drop links (~NT$25,000)
Out-of-warranty BEV risk budget - electric coolant pump, thermal-management valves, charge-port actuator, HV sensor faults (~NT$25,000 expected value)
Two annual services at full BMW dealer rates plus brake fluid and coolant (~NT$32,000)
Air-conditioning service and cabin blower (~NT$8,000), filters, wipers, alignment (~NT$6,000)
checkpoints.source: REVISED UP from NT$128,000 to absorb the brake pads correctly moved out of year 5. Extrapolated from BMW Taiwan dealer labour rates and the U-CAR consumable benchmark (article 77119), uplifted for premium-German parts pricing. No engine-side items apply (no oil, plugs, coil packs, thermostat housing or DPF on a BEV), but the electric coolant pump and thermal-management hardware are the direct BEV equivalents of that risk class and are included. Deliberately far above a Japanese equivalent: this is a German premium BEV with no warranty backstop on anything except the high-voltage battery.

major_items: 8-year/160,000 km high-voltage battery warranty EXPIRES at year 8 - the whole window is unprotected
Drive unit / inverter / HV component risk budget (~NT$40,000 expected value)
Suspension refresh on a 2-tonne BEV: dampers, top mounts, bushings (~NT$55,000)
Electric A/C compressor - a costly and common BEV failure since it also feeds battery cooling (~NT$28,000 expected value)
Electric coolant pump / thermal-management module (~NT$30,000)
On-board charger and AC charge-port faults (~NT$25,000 expected value)
SECOND FULL TIRE SET on age (~NT$40,000) plus second 12V battery (~NT$15,000) and brake pads/discs top-up (~NT$20,000)
Three annual services, two brake-fluid changes, coolant, filters, wipers, alignment, misc electronics (~NT$52,000)
checkpoints.source: Extrapolated over a three-year window with no warranty of any kind remaining. This is the period the honest model must not understate: a decade-old German BEV in Taiwan carries thermal-management, HV-electronics and charging-hardware exposure that a naturally-aspirated Japanese SUV simply does not, and BMW dealer labour is roughly double the Korean-brand basis U-CAR published. The BEV genuinely saves the engine-side items (no water pump, coil packs, thermostat housing or DPF), which is why the 10-year total of ~NT$549,000 is not higher still - but it is multiples of a RAV4's, which is the correct outcome. Figures are risk-weighted expected values, not worst cases.

assumptions.notes: Buyer drives 6,000-8,000 km/year; all checkpoints use 7,000 km/year (7,000 / 21,000 / 35,000 / 49,000 / 70,000 km) - roughly half the Taiwan average, so servicing is time-driven (annual visits) rather than mileage-driven. TIMING CAVEAT: as of 2026-08-12 this car is not yet on sale in Taiwan. BMW TW (agent 汎德) opened online pre-order in May 2026 (NT$100,000 deposit, 50 xDrive only), dealer-sourced pre-sale prices surfaced 2026-06-05, a media preview was held 2026-07-20, and formal launch is October 2026. The 50 xDrive delivers from ~November 2026; THE 40 M SPORT DOES NOT DELIVER UNTIL JANUARY 2027, so year 1 of ownership effectively runs 2027-2028 and every downstream figure is shifted about a year later than the model_year 2026 label implies. Home-charger installation is deliberately EXCLUDED from maintenance per the brief - budget roughly NT$40,000-80,000 separately for a BMW Wallbox plus installation, plus building/管委會 approval in an apartment. Electricity, insurance and tax are also excluded by design; note that Taiwan BEVs currently enjoy 牌照稅/燃料費 exemptions and 貨物稅 relief, none of which are counted here.

purchase.source: Independently re-verified 2026-08-12 by fetching U-CAR directly: the iX3 model page (newcar.u-car.com.tw/bmw/ix3/7254/overall) shows the range as 280-325 萬 with '40 M Sport 280' in the trim table, and U-CAR news 88833 (2026-06-05) and 89191 (2026-07-20) both state 預售價 280 萬 / 325 萬. purchase.notes: True BEV: 800V Neue Klasse platform (chassis code NA5), single rear motor (後輪驅動), 320 hp, 86.9 kWh battery per U-CAR, WLTP 637 km, 300 kW DC peak, CCS2 for Taiwan. CORRECTION vs the reviewed record, which stated '82.6 kWh usable / WLTP 636 km' in conflict with its own cited source: U-CAR publishes 86.9 kWh and 637 km for the 40. Usable capacity for the 40 is NOT published; ~82-83 kWh is an inference from the 50 xDrive's published 113.4 kWh gross / 108.4 kWh usable ratio, so it is stated as an inference here rather than as spec. No 48V/hybrid ambiguity - this is unambiguously 'bev'. PRICE STATUS: NT$2,800,000 is provisional. BMW Taiwan moves the number at launch in both directions - the facelift i4 eDrive40 went from a 277 萬 pre-sale to a 275 萬 list (-NT$20,000) and then to 279 萬 for the 2026 年式, so treat NT$2,800,000 as roughly +NT$50,000 / -NT$20,000 uncertain. DISCOUNTS SET TO ZERO, deliberately. Over 1,200 orders are banked with nothing delivered and the 40 has a queue running into 2027 (both figures confirmed in U-CAR 89191); nobody discounts a car in that position. BMW TW competes with non-price sweeteners instead - its January 2025 'BMW i 榮耀共享' campaign gave 2-3 years of unlimited U-POWER charging plus a 4th-year extended warranty on iX/i4/iX1 rather than cutting price - so the warranty perk is reflected in maintenance instead. Note the 40 is the unpopular half of the range: confirmed order split is 80% 50 xDrive / 20% 40 M Sport, which hurts used-market liquidity later. ONROAD_FEES NT$85,000 (~3% of list) = 領牌+代辦 ~NT$15,000 plus ~NT$70,000 of accessories every car in this class leaves with in Taiwan: ceramic window film on a large-glass BEV (NT$25,000-40,000), paint coating (a real BMW iX owner logged NT$18,000 for 鍍膜), dashcam, mats and cargo tray. Excludes tax and insurance by design. real_cost = 2,800,000 - 0 + 85,000.

value_checkpoints.source: EXTRAPOLATED - no used data for this car can exist (first 40 M Sport delivers January 2027). CORRECTED DOWN from the reviewed record's NT$2,135,000 (76.3% of list), which cherry-picked only the strongest proxies and several 原廠認證中古車 (BPS-certified) listings that carry a certification premium. I re-pulled auto.8891.com.tw/bmw/i on 2026-08-12 and used the full spread of genuinely low-mileage 1-1.5-year BMW BEVs, each against its own original TW list: iX2 xDrive30 M Sport (orig NT$2,370,000) at 3,000 km NT$2,050,000, 5,800 km NT$2,000,000, 5,801 km NT$2,030,000 = 84-87%; i4 eDrive40 facelift (orig NT$2,750,000) NON-certified at 5,900-5,978 km NT$2,280,000 = 83%, versus certified examples at NT$2,430,000-2,450,000 = 88-89% (the ~5-point BPS premium the reviewed record failed to strip out); i5 eDrive40 M Sport (orig NT$3,290,000) at 5,000 km NT$2,500,000 = 76%. EXTRAPOLATED from real 3-year-old German BEV listings re-pulled from auto.8891.com.tw/bmw/i on 2026-08-12. EXTRAPOLATED - no 7-year-old German BEV of this class exists in the Taiwan used market at all, so this is interpolated between the year-5 figure and the genuine 9-11 year BMW i3 evidence below, on a curve that keeps falling rather than flattening. 31.8% of list / 30.9% of real_cost, i.e. the car keeps only 70.6% of its year-5 value across years 5-7 versus 80.3% across years 3-5 - the decline accelerates rather than plateauing. EXTRAPOLATED from the only genuine 10-year German BEV data in Taiwan, and MATERIALLY CORRECTED. The reviewed record used NT$2,390,000 as the i3 denominator, but all four live 8891 i3 listings (re-pulled 2026-08-12: 2017 REx 140,000 km NT$520,000; 2016 REx 83,000 km NT$598,000; 2016 REx 90,000 km NT$458,000; 2015 REx 110,000 km NT$458,000) are 增程式 REx cars, and U-CAR's 2014 launch article prices the i3 純電 at NT$2,390,000 but the i3 REx at NT$2,990,000 - a NT$600,000 gap driven by 貨物稅 treatment. Against the correct NT$2,990,000 denominator these ask 15.3-20.0%, averaging 17.0% of list at DEALER RETAIL, not the 19-25% claimed. Converting to private sale (-12%) gives ~15.0%. I set 16.4% of list (15.9% of real_cost), credited above the raw read for our car's much lower 70,000 km and its larger, more modern platform, but NOT to the reviewed record's 19.6% - which was both built on the wrong denominator and set at essentially dealer-retail level. Note the i3 REx proxy is if anything flattering: it carries a petrol range-extender that removes battery anxiety (one listing advertises exactly that) while keeping 電動車牌 tax status, an upside our pure BEV will not have. The dominant tail risk stands: the 8-year/160,000 km HV battery warranty expires at year 8, and an out-of-warranty ~83 kWh pack on a 10-year-old car costs more to replace than the car is worth. Dealer trade-in a further -18% - dealers discount old BEVs hardest because they are slow to move and carry pack risk.

maintenance.plan_notes: Servicing is TIME-DRIVEN, not mileage-driven, at 7,000 km/year: the car calls for an annual (condition-based CBS) visit long before any distance trigger, and reaches only 70,000 km by year 10. Costs are anchored on a real BMW Taiwan dealer invoice for a BMW iX xDrive40 (桃園大桐 BMW 經銷商, 2024, 2-year/40,019 km service) shared on the PTT car board: NT$5,931 before tax, NT$6,228 invoiced, comprising 車輛保養檢查 NT$1,050, 保養標準範圍 NT$420, 風箱清潔劑 NT$1,875, plus a brake-fluid service at NT$2,586; BMW TW labour bills at NT$210 per unit. CAVEAT ON THAT SOURCE: the itemised line amounts and the '10 mm pad thickness at 40,000 km' reading exist only in imgur invoice photos attached to the thread and cannot be re-verified from the thread text; what the owner's own prose does confirm is that after two years '煞車皮也沒什麼磨損' and that the dealer's 冷氣濾網 line was deleted because the owner sourced the same German filter for NT$3,000 + NT$200 fitting. Minimal pad wear is consistent with BMW's published claim - verified on U-CAR - that up to 98% of everyday braking on the iX3 is handled by the Heart of Joy regeneration system. So no pad wear is budgeted on mileage; instead the years 5-7 and 7-10 windows carry DISC REPLACEMENT ON CORROSION, the classic failure mode for a low-mileage BEV in Taiwan's humidity. TIRES ARE THE BIG BEV CONSUMABLE and the same owner proves it: on a heavy BMW BEV the original tires were worn to the wear bar and replaced all four inside the FIRST year at just over 30,000 km, for NT$56,000 at the dealer on 21-inch fitment. At 7,000 km/year that puts our first set at year 5 (35,000 km) and the second at year 10 (70,000 km) - wear and age happen to coincide. WARRANTY: BMW TW gives 3 years unlimited mileage on the car and 8 years/160,000 km on the HV battery, and its BMW i campaigns routinely add a 4th-year extended warranty (e.g. the January 2025 'BMW i 榮耀共享' promo on iX/i4/iX1). Years 1 and 3 are therefore scheduled servicing only. Critically, BMW Taiwan does NOT bundle free scheduled maintenance - the owner pays at every visit, as the invoice above shows - and the years 5, 7 and 10 periods carry the FULL unsubsidised cost including out-of-warranty risk provisions. NOT APPLICABLE because this is a true BEV, contrary to the generic German-car checklist: no engine oil, no spark plugs, no coil packs, no thermostat housing, no DPF, and no 48V starter-generator. Air suspension is also excluded - it is not offered on the iX3 NA5 at all (unlike the iX and X5), and the 40 M Sport rides on conventional springs. What replaces them are BEV-specific items: battery and power-electronics coolant, the electric coolant pump, the HV battery cooling compressor, the on-board charger and charge port, the 12V battery (which still dies on schedule), and faster-wearing tires on a ~2,285 kg car. Total 10-year maintenance NT$528,000 - roughly 2.5 to 3 times a RAV4, but well under a combustion X3, which is the honest position for a German luxury BEV. All figures are 2024-2026 prices applied to 2027-2037 spending, so they are if anything conservative.

assumptions.notes: Buyer drives 6,000-8,000 km/yr, roughly half the Taiwan average of 12,000-15,000 km/yr. Every checkpoint uses assumed_km = 7000 x years (7,000 / 21,000 / 35,000 / 49,000 / 70,000). Tax (牌照稅/燃料稅) and insurance are excluded by design and appear nowhere in this record. Fuel is also not modelled - only purchase, resale and maintenance. All figures are TWD. The car's 48V mild-hybrid system is a starter-generator that cannot propel the car on battery alone, so powertrain is 'gasoline'; it is not a full hybrid. No home-charger or energy costs apply (not a BEV/PHEV).

purchase.notes: PRICE: NT$2,200,000 confirmed against three independently fetched or quoted sources. Price history: the U11 launched in Taiwan 2023-02-23 at sDrive18i xLine NT$1,900,000 / sDrive20i xLine NT$2,120,000 / iX1 xDrive30 NT$2,220,000; 汎德 raised X1 prices by NT$40,000 in Sept 2023 (20i xLine to NT$2,160,000); the M Sport Edition replaced xLine in Nov 2025 at NT$2,200,000. The 48V hardware still matters for cost and is carried explicitly in the later maintenance windows. DISCOUNT NT$70,000: the X1 is BMW TW's volume compact SUV and the M Sport Edition is a freshly repriced, value-added trim, so cash room is moderate rather than deep - typical negotiated cash off runs NT$50,000-90,000, and 汎德 prefers to bundle a BSI service package and accessories instead of cutting price. Mid-band taken. ON-ROAD NT$58,000 = 領牌/監理規費 ~NT$4,000 + 代辦費 ~NT$8,000 + 配件 (window film, dashcam, floor mats, coating) ~NT$46,000, scaled to a NT$2.2M premium SUV. CORRECTED UPWARD from the researcher's NT$1,310,000 - their figure was internally impossible. Real 2023-2024 U11 sDrive20i listings found: (a) 2023 sDrive20i xLine, 出廠 2023/01, 35,749 km, asking NT$1,450,000 as a genuine 自售 PRIVATE listing; (b) 2023 sDrive20i, 56,862 km (built 2023/01, reg 2023/04), DEALER asking NT$1,480,000; (c) 2024 sDrive20i, 16,427 km, BMW Premium Selection 原廠認證, DEALER asking NT$1,660,000. The researcher derived a dealer-retail asking price of NT$1,455,000 for a 21,000 km three-year car - BELOW the observed NT$1,480,000 dealer ask on a 56,862 km car of the same model year, and below the NT$1,450,000 PRIVATE ask on a 35,749 km car of the same model year. A lower-mileage car of the same vintage cannot be worth less, so that anchor is wrong. Corrected build-up: a 2023-vintage 20i with 21,000 km, non-certified, sits between (b) and (c) at ~NT$1,570,000 dealer retail asking; less ~10% = NT$1,420,000 private sale; less a further ~13% = NT$1,230,000 trade-in. Cross-check from the other direction: comp (a) is a real private ask at NT$1,450,000 for a car that is 0.4 yr older, 14,749 km higher and on a lower NT$2,120,000 list - after knocking ~4% off asking to reach a realised price and adjusting for age, mileage and trim, that route also lands ~NT$1,450,000-1,520,000. NT$1,420,000 is the conservative end of the converged range. ~65% of real_cost at year 3.

EXTRAPOLATED - no five-year-old U11 exists (this generation only launched in Taiwan 2023-02), so real PREDECESSOR F48 X1 used prices at this age were converted to a retention ratio against the F48's own original list and applied to this car. F48 evidence at 5-6 years old: a 2021 sDrive20i low-mileage top-spec asking NT$1,298,000; a 2020 sDrive20i (built 2019/10, reg 2020/04) 34,072 km BMW-certified asking NT$900,000; a 2020 at NT$1,030,000; a 2020 with 46,000 km asking NT$1,388,000 (high outlier, not anchored on); FindCar averages of NT$948,000 (2021) and NT$962,000 across 13 2020 cars. Average cars sit near NT$950,000 but our 35,000 km car is well under average mileage and belongs at the TOP of the band, so ~NT$1,290,000 dealer retail asking on an F48-equivalent basis (~62% of the F48's ~NT$2,090,000 list). Applied to this car: ~NT$1,310,000 dealer retail asking, less ~10% = NT$1,180,000 private sale, less a further ~14% = NT$1,010,000 trade-in. ~54% of real_cost. Set slightly below a pure ratio transfer because the U11's 1,499cc three-cylinder plus 48V drivetrain is less trusted in the Taiwan used market than the F48's 2.0-litre four - TW owner threads explicitly cite avoiding '48V 的維修機率' as a reason to buy the 18i over the 20i.

EXTRAPOLATED from the predecessor F48 generation, same ratio-transfer method. Real F48 evidence at 7 years old (2019 model year): a 2019 F48 at a Taichung dealer asking NT$869,000, with TW dealer asking averages clustering ~NT$880,000 and clean low-mileage examples reaching ~NT$1,100,000, against a ~NT$1,970,000 F48 sDrive20i list - about 45% of original list on dealer asking for an average car, ~56% for a clean low-mileage one. Our 49,000 km car at 7 years is far below the typical 90,000-100,000 km, so the low-mileage end applies rather than the average: ~NT$1,070,000 implied dealer retail asking, less ~10% = NT$960,000 private sale, less a further ~16% = NT$810,000 trade-in. ~44% of real_cost. The researcher applied the BOTTOM of the F48 band (~40%) to a genuinely low-mileage car, which contradicts the low-mileage buyer profile; corrected to the low-mileage end but still below a pure ratio transfer, because by year 7 the car is outside BMW TW's warranty and outside any BSI package, and the used market prices in 48V starter-generator, electric water pump and 7-speed DCT risk on this drivetrain. The German tail keeps falling here instead of flattening the way a Lexus does.

EXTRAPOLATED from the predecessor F48 generation. Real F48 evidence at 10 years old (2016 model year, sDrive20i): Taiwan dealer askings of NT$458,000, NT$578,000 (80,000 km), NT$599,000 and NT$718,000 for a well-kept example, against the F48's NT$1,890,000 launch list - roughly 30-38% of original list on DEALER ASKING for a decent car. A cross-generation valuation summary puts the whole F48 generation (2015-2022) at a ~NT$538,000 median and the E84 (2010-2015) at ~NT$288,000, consistent with that band. Applied ~33% of list on dealer asking for a 70,000 km ten-year car, which is well under average mileage: ~NT$722,000 implied dealer asking, less ~10% = NT$650,000 private sale, less a further ~18% = NT$530,000 trade-in. ~30% of real_cost. The private-to-trade-in percentage spread widens on cheap old cars because dealers need a roughly fixed absolute margin. The low-mileage credit is partly offset by the three-cylinder/48V repair-risk discount and the fact that a decade-old out-of-warranty BMW in Taiwan is priced on fear rather than condition.

maintenance.plan_notes: TIME-DRIVEN, NOT MILEAGE-DRIVEN. At 7,000 km/yr this car never reaches BMW's CBS (Condition Based Service - the car computes its own service intervals from sensors and usage) distance trigger of roughly 15,000-25,000 km for engine oil. Servicing is therefore effectively annual on the calendar, and BMW TW dealers push annual servicing regardless because Taiwan's heat, humidity and short-trip city use degrade oil faster than distance suggests. Brake fluid stays on its fixed 2-year cycle, coolant and spark plugs come due on age long before mileage, and tires are replaced on rubber age (~5-6 years) rather than tread depth - hence two full tire sets in ten years despite only 70,000 km. BSI IS A PROMOTION, NOT STANDARD EQUIPMENT - this is a correction. The researcher booked years 1 and 3 at NT$6,000 and NT$16,000 on the assumption that a BSI (BMW Service Inclusive) 3年/60,000公里 保養套裝 is bundled with the deal. Checking BMW TW dealer material, that package is consistently advertised as '限時加贈3年/6萬公里BSI原廠保養套裝' and '本月交車領牌更限時加贈' - i.e. a limited-time 加贈 promotion tied to whatever month you take delivery, not 標配. It cannot be assumed for a buyer transacting at an arbitrary date, so years 1 and 3 have been raised to NT$12,000 and NT$26,000, which is roughly the midpoint between a fully BSI-covered outcome and paying 原廠 rates out of pocket. If BSI IS on the deal, subtract about NT$20,000 across years 1-3; if it is not, add about NT$10,000. BMW TW's 3年不限里程 new-car warranty still covers defects in that window either way, which is why these periods stay low in absolute terms. YEARS 5, 7 AND 10 CARRY THE FULL UNSUBSIDISED DEALER COST - no package, no warranty, and repair risk priced in. All figures assume 原廠 (authorised dealer) pricing; a competent 外廠 independent BMW specialist typically runs 40-50% cheaper on the years-5-to-10 windows, which is what most Taiwanese owners actually switch to once the warranty lapses. Ten-year total lands near NT$478,000 - roughly double what an equivalent Japanese compact SUV would cost over the same period, which is the correct shape for a German premium car and is driven by dealer labour rates, 19-inch runflat tires, larger brakes, and out-of-warranty risk items specific to the B38 three-cylinder and its 48V hardware.

major_items: First annual service at 原廠 - engine oil, oil filter, inspection
Wiper blades
Wheel alignment / tire pressure and TPMS check
Washer fluid and minor consumables
checkpoints.source: RAISED from the researcher's NT$6,000. Their figure assumed the BSI 3年/60,000公里 package covers the first service; BMW TW material advertises that package as a limited-time 加贈 promotion ('限時加贈3年/6萬公里BSI原廠保養套裝'), not 標配, so it cannot be assumed. Real TW owner invoices for a dealer oil service: NT$4,834 on a BMW 220i at 7,820 km, and ~NT$6,000 for oil + oil filter + labour reported by another owner; TW owner threads put in-warranty basic servicing 'under NT$10,000' a year. NT$12,000 is the midpoint between a BSI-covered year (~NT$4,000 of uncovered consumables) and a fully out-of-pocket 原廠 year (~NT$10,000-12,000 with wipers and alignment). Defects remain covered by the standard 3年不限里程 warranty either way.

major_items: Two annual services (years 2 and 3) at 原廠 - oil, oil filter, air filter, cabin filter
Brake fluid change at year 2 (fixed 2-year interval)
Wiper blades x2 sets
Wheel alignment

checkpoints.source: RAISED from the researcher's NT$16,000, same reason as year 1 - the BSI package is a limited-time promotion, not standard equipment, so two years of servicing cannot be assumed free. Build-up at 原廠 rates: two annual services at ~NT$8,000 each = NT$16,000, brake fluid ~NT$3,500, wipers/alignment/consumables ~NT$5,000, A/C and minor checks ~NT$5,000, giving ~NT$29,500 fully out of pocket; NT$26,000 books a partial-BSI expectation. Service pricing anchored on real TW owner invoices (NT$4,834 oil-only, ~NT$6,000 oil + filter + labour) plus filters. Spark plugs are nominally a BSI item but at 21,000 km over three years they are nowhere near the ~60,000 km interval, so they fall into the 3-5 year window instead, on age. Mechanical defects are still warranty-covered in this window.

major_items: First tire set replaced on AGE not tread - 4x 19-inch M runflat + fitting and alignment, ~NT$40,000
Front brake pads + wear sensor at dealer, ~NT$13,000
Spark plugs x3 (time-based, B38 three-cylinder), ~NT$9,000
12V AGM battery + registration to the car, ~NT$12,000
Two post-warranty dealer annual services (oil, oil filter, air filter, cabin filter), ~NT$16,000
Brake fluid change (2-year cycle), ~NT$3,500
Wipers, alignment, misc consumables
checkpoints.source: This is the first fully unsubsidised window - the 3年不限里程 warranty and any BSI package both expired at year 3, which is why the cost jumps by an order of magnitude. Tires: Taiwan retail for 225/55R18 runflat starts ~NT$4,222/tire for budget Hankook (~NT$16,888 fitted for four with free 3D alignment); the M Sport's 19-inch premium runflats (Bridgestone/Michelin/Pirelli) run NT$8,500-10,000 each, so ~NT$40,000 for four fitted and aligned. Brakes: a TW BMW dealer quote for front+rear pads is ~NT$26,000 (independents quote NT$13,000 OEM-equivalent or NT$7,000 Textar); front-only booked here. Annual service: NT$8,000/visit at dealer, extrapolated from reported NT$4,834-6,000 oil-only invoices plus filters. Battery and plug pricing from TW BMW parts/labour norms. Modelled expectation, not an observed invoice.

major_items: Front discs + second pad set, ~NT$22,000 (BMW discs wear with the pads and rarely survive two sets)
Rear brake pads + wear sensor, ~NT$11,000
7-speed dual-clutch (DCT) oil and filter service, ~NT$16,000 - BMW calls it lifetime, TW specialists do not
Electric water pump / thermostat housing, probability-weighted ~NT$16,000
Coolant change, ~NT$6,000
Front control-arm bushings, ~NT$12,000
Two dealer annual services, ~NT$18,000
Brake fluid, wipers, 48V system diagnostics, misc, ~NT$9,000
checkpoints.source: Extrapolated from Taiwan BMW out-of-warranty repair norms rather than from a published table - no official TW price list for these items is public. Item selection is grounded in the documented failure profile of the B38 three-cylinder and its cooling system: TW/JP owner discussions and repair sites cite the electric water pump (impeller damage causing poor cooling, seal ageing causing coolant leaks) and ignition coils as the recurring BMW items at this age. Dealer brake pricing anchored on the ~NT$26,000 front+rear pad quote reported by TW owners, with individual OEM front pad sets with sensor at NT$5,100-5,200 and discs at NT$2,700-4,300. Water pump and control arms are probability-weighted, not booked at full cost, because they do not fail on every car. Low confidence: these are modelled expectations for a car this age, not observed invoices for a 2026 U11 (which cannot exist yet).

major_items: Second tire set (age-driven again) - 4x 19-inch runflat fitted, ~NT$42,000
48V starter-generator / 48V lithium battery - the mild-hybrid's signature big-ticket risk, probability-weighted ~NT$22,000 (full replacement is NT$60,000-90,000 at dealer)
Oil leaks: valve-cover gasket + oil-filter-housing gasket, the classic BMW pair at this age, ~NT$25,000
Rear discs + pads, ~NT$20,000
Ignition coils x3 (known B38 weak point), ~NT$12,000
Water pump / thermostat if not already replaced in the 5-7 window, ~NT$15,000
Second 12V AGM battery, ~NT$13,000
Dampers - M Sport sport suspension, probability-weighted ~NT$18,000
Three dealer annual services, ~NT$27,000
Second spark plug set ~NT$10,000, brake fluid x2 ~NT$7,000, A/C, sensors and electrical misc ~NT$19,000
checkpoints.source: Extrapolated. Works out to ~NT$77,000/yr across the 7-10 window, the realistic shape for an out-of-warranty German premium SUV in Taiwan and deliberately far above what a RAV4 or CX-5 would cost over the same three years. The 48V starter-generator allowance is the item that most distinguishes this car from a plain-gasoline equivalent and is the reason Taiwanese buyers on owner forums openly choose the sDrive18i to avoid '48V 的維修機率'. Big-ticket risk items are probability-weighted rather than booked in full, so this is an expected value, not a worst case - a car that needs the ISG outright plus dampers could exceed NT$320,000 in this window, while a lucky one might come in near NT$150,000. No genuine 10-year data exists for this generation; this is a modelled figure built from TW BMW dealer labour and parts norms and the documented failure profile of the B38 + 48V drivetrain. The NT$60,000-90,000 ISG replacement range and the ~30% failure probability behind the NT$22,000 expected value are estimates, not sourced invoices - this is the single largest modelled item in the table.

assumptions.notes: Buyer drives 6,000-8,000 km/year; every checkpoint uses assumed_km = 7000 * years (7,000 / 21,000 / 35,000 / 49,000 / 70,000), far below the Taiwan average of ~12,000-15,000 km/year. Because of this, used values are taken from LOW-MILEAGE listings rather than mileage-blind averages, and servicing is treated as time-driven (annual) rather than mileage-driven - the car never reaches BMW's mileage-based CBS intervals within a year. POWERTRAIN: the sDrive20i uses the B38 1.5L turbo 3-cylinder with a 48V ISG mild-hybrid system (156 hp engine + 19 hp ISG = 170 hp combined). It CANNOT move on battery alone, so it is classified 'gasoline', not 'hybrid'. Vehicle tax, insurance and fuel are excluded from every figure by design. All used figures start from dealer-retail asking prices observed on 8891 and are converted DOWN to private-sale and then trade-in level (see each value_checkpoints source string). Used supply of the current U10 generation in Taiwan is genuinely thin - a nationwide 8891 X2 search returns ~40 cars on the first page across both generations, of which 10 are U10 - so near-new asking prices are sticky rather than market-clearing, which is why a wide 12-13% haircut is applied to reach private-sale level.
